proposals.relationship: Wheeler uses Ahenakew’s written Old Keyam narrative to show why interpreting recorded Cree knowledge requires its language, relationships and cultural contexts (2018).
proposals.evidence_note: A situated resource for oral-history interpretation, not a claim that Ahenakew founded the modern field. Wheeler credits Maria Campbell’s interpretation of coded teachings; Campbell’s unpublished 1999 paper is unread. Thunderchild’s narration, Ahenakew’s writing and Ruth Buck’s later editing remain distinct.
primary_locators: Wheeler2018 paragraphs beginning “Another example”, “Ahenakew brilliantly”, “On the surface” through “Scholars need”; notes6–12.

proposals.relationship: In her 2003 review, Beatrice Medicine identifies Ahenakew among the Indigenous scholars whose historical insights inform Carter’s 1999 survey.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicitly attributed scholarly review of Aboriginal People and Colonizers of Western Canada to 1900; the book body remains unread. This records reported use of historical insight, not mentorship, exclusive influence or a verified particular Ahenakew work. Medicine’s Big Bear example and Christine Welsh’s formulation are not assigned to Ahenakew.
primary_locators: Medicine’s signed review printed196–197, especially197 paragraph beginning “Drawing upon an ethnohistorical method”; PDF pages2–3 one-based.
